planting.note: Press seed into moist, sandy, humus-poor soil in fall; this coastal-plain violet wants the lean, acidic conditions of pine woods rather than rich garden loam.

directions: Dark violet to blue (occasionally white) flowers with a hairless petal throat open from March into May above deeply lobed, hairy-margined leaves, drawing in early-season mining bees and other small pollinators. The species is a true coastal-plain specialist, tracking sandy, fire-maintained longleaf pine and mixed pine-hardwood woodlands from the Louisiana-Mississippi line east across the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains. It wants dappled light under an open pine canopy and sharply drained, acidic sand rather than the richer, moister soil preferred by most deep-shade violets, and it resents heavy mulch or compost piled against the crown. Established clumps slowly thicken by short rhizomes and tolerate the periodic low fire that keeps its pine-woodland habitat open.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: A federally threatened Florida Panhandle endemic found nowhere else on Earth; source only nursery-propagated division stock from a specialist native plant grower and never collect or disturb wild colonies, which survive in just four counties.

directions: Tight, nest-like terminal clusters of white, purple-flecked, two-lipped mint flowers open from June into August above an upright, square-stemmed clump, and bumblebees are the primary pollinators working the tubular blooms. This exceptionally rare member of the mint family is restricted entirely to wet-to-mesic pine flatwoods, seepage bogs, and roadside ditches of the Apalachicola National Forest region in the Florida Panhandle, a habitat that depends on frequent, low-intensity fire to stay open. Site it in consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil with only light shade from scattered pine canopy, since fire suppression and woody encroachment are the main threats to the species in the wild. Because so few populations remain, any garden planting should rely strictly on nursery-propagated material, never wild-collected plants.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in constantly moist, acidic, organic soil along a seep or streamside edge with at least a half-day of direct sun; too much shade produces lanky, floppy stems that fall over before bloom.

directions: Strongly recurved, nodding, orange-yellow flowers heavily spotted with maroon open atop tall stems in July and August, their Turk's-cap shape and bright color drawing swallowtail butterflies and hummingbirds. The species is confined to seepage slopes, pitcher-plant bogs, and blackwater stream edges of the western Florida Panhandle and two adjoining Alabama counties, almost always growing alongside Sarracenia pitcher plants in boggy, continuously saturated sand. It needs the bright, open light of a flatwoods-wetland ecotone rather than closed-canopy shade, and populations are vulnerable to ditching, fire suppression, and development that disrupts the seepage hydrology it depends on. Mulch lightly and keep the root zone wet through summer to mimic its native seep habitat.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Like other grapeferns it depends on a soil mycorrhizal partner and cannot be reliably seed-propagated; transplant only nursery-grown divisions into undisturbed, humus-rich loam and expect a long, unpredictable establishment period.

directions: This small, unusual fern runs on the opposite calendar from almost everything else in a Gulf South garden: its single fleshy, divided blade emerges in fall once the hardwood canopy has thinned, stays green through winter catching the extra light, and then withers away by late spring long before summer heat arrives. It occurs across the Gulf Coastal Plain from Texas and Louisiana through Mississippi, Alabama, and the Florida Panhandle, typically in the loamy, leaf-littered soil of bottomland hardwood forests and old fields rather than deep permanent shade. Like its grapefern relatives it depends on an underground mycorrhizal fungus to survive and resents soil disturbance, so established colonies should be left undisturbed once sited. Its reproductive spike is easy to overlook among fallen leaves, making it one of the more quietly overlooked natives of winter bottomland woods.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Cultivation is effectively impossible: this orchid has no chlorophyll and survives only by parasitizing a specific soil fungus tied to the surrounding trees, so wild-dug plants always die and no viable nursery propagation method exists.

directions: This record exists for identification purposes only, not as a cultivation guide: Spring Coralroot sends up a leafless, brownish-purple flowering stalk from a coral-like underground rhizome, with small purplish-brown flowers appearing in late winter through early spring while most of the surrounding woodland is still bare. It occurs in humus-rich leaf litter under moist deciduous and mixed woods across a broad range that reaches Louisiana and Texas at its Gulf Coast edge. Having no green tissue, it draws all of its carbon and nutrients from mycorrhizal fungi in the soil, which makes transplanting fatal and intentional cultivation unworkable. If you find it on your property, the best action is to leave the leaf litter and canopy trees undisturbed rather than attempt to move or propagate it.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
Go Orchids (North American Orchid Conservation Center)

planting.note: This orchid is rare, mycorrhizae-dependent, and essentially uncultivable outside its native leaf litter; never collect from the wild, and treat any naturally occurring colony as a feature to protect in place rather than move.

directions: This record is included for identification and conservation awareness rather than as garden guidance: translucent, waxy little stems carry small clusters of pale pink to white flowers that famously open in synchrony across an entire colony on the same morning, each individual bloom lasting only a single day, typically in late summer. It grows half-buried in deep leaf litter on the floor of mature, moist deciduous forests, with a range that reaches from the Florida Panhandle west to Texas along the Gulf Coastal Plain. Its dependence on a soil mycorrhizal partner and its habit of lying dormant underground for years between appearances make it unsuitable for transplanting or deliberate cultivation. Protecting intact leaf litter and canopy shade is the only real way to support a population that happens to occur on a wooded property.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
